title: Grinds and Slides Step by Step
bigQuestion: How does a skater go from rolling past a curb to sliding along it with control?

story.title: The First Scrape
story.kicker: A skater waxes a painted curb and hears her trucks grind for the very first time.
paragraphs: Marisol kneels beside the low painted curb at the edge of the skatepark's flat area. The curb is about as tall as her shoe is long. She pulls a small block of skate wax from her pocket and rubs it along the top edge in short strokes. A thin, shiny film builds up on the yellow paint. She tests it with a fingertip. It feels slick, almost greasy.

She buckles her helmet and checks that it sits low on her forehead, two fingers above her eyebrows. Wrist guards, knee pads, flat shoes. For weeks she has practiced her ollie on the open concrete until she could pop it while rolling every time. Today she wants to put that ollie on top of the curb.

She pushes off slowly and rides beside the curb, close and almost parallel, the way her coach showed her. On the first three tries she only ollies up onto the curb top and rolls off again. Her coach nods and says that is exactly the right first step. On the fourth try she aims her board at the edge itself, keeps her knees bent and looks at the far end of the curb instead of at her feet.

Both trucks land on the corner of the curb. For a moment she hears a long, rough scrape, metal on painted concrete, and feels a buzz come up through her shoes. Then the board slows and tips off the side. She steps off with both feet, jogs a few steps and laughs. It lasted barely a meter, but it was a grind. She walks back to the start, rubs on a little more wax and lines up again.
story.think: Marisol practiced ollying onto the curb before she tried to grind it. Why might that smaller step help her feel ready?

lessons.title: Grinds, Slides and a Safe Start
lessons.mainIdea: A grind rides on the trucks and a slide rides on the deck, and both start on something low with your gear on.
reading: Skaters use two words for riding along an edge. In a *grind*, the metal trucks scrape along the edge. The axle and the hanger, the T-shaped metal part that holds the axle, take the contact. In a *slide*, the wooden underside of the deck rubs along the edge instead. Both tricks use a *ledge*, a long edge like a curb or a concrete block, or a *rail*, a metal bar or pipe.

Start low. A painted curb at a skatepark or a flat bar a few inches off the ground is the right first obstacle. A flat bar is a straight metal rail that sits level, close to the ground, on short legs. If you fall from a low curb, you only drop a short way. Stairs, handrails and tall ledges come much later, at a skatepark, when a skater has years of control.

Before you try, put on a helmet that fits snugly and is buckled, plus wrist guards and knee pads. Wear flat-soled shoes that grip the grip tape. Pick a dry, smooth place away from cars and away from people walking. Most grinds and slides need a steady ollie while rolling, so practice that first. If your ollie gets you a few inches off flat ground every time, you are ready to begin.

words.d: a trick in which one or both metal trucks scrape along an edge or rail
a trick in which the wooden underside of the deck rubs along an edge or rail
a long, raised edge such as a curb or concrete block that skaters grind or slide on
a metal bar or pipe that skaters grind or slide on

lessons.title: Wax on the Edge
lessons.mainIdea: Skate wax makes an edge slicker so the board slides farther, and a thin coat is enough.
reading: New concrete and fresh paint can grab a board and stop it short. Skaters fix this with *wax*. Skate wax comes in small blocks sold for skating. Some skaters use plain paraffin, the kind of wax used in candles. Rub the block along the top corner of the ledge in short strokes, then rub it in with the side of the block until the edge looks shiny.

A thin coat works best. Too little and the trucks still catch. Too much and the edge gets so slick the board can shoot out from under you, or it builds up in sticky lumps. Try one run, then add a little more if the board stops short. Wax wears off as people skate, so a ledge may need a fresh coat after a session.

Wax only edges where skating is allowed, like the curbs and ledges at a skatepark. Wax leaves marks and can make a public step slippery for people walking. A good habit is to bring your own small block, wax just the edge you are using, and leave the area as clean as you found it. Wax also works on a flat bar, though metal rails are already smoother than concrete.

words.d: a slippery coating rubbed on an edge so a board slides along it more easily
a plain, colorless wax, like candle wax, that some skaters use on edges
a stretch of time spent skating one spot or practicing one trick

to make the edge slicker so the board slides farther
to paint the edge a new color
check.why: Wax makes the edge slick, so trucks and decks slide farther.

check.q: What can happen if a skater puts on far too much wax?
choices: the board can shoot out or the wax builds into sticky lumps
check.why: Too much wax makes the edge overly slick or lumpy, so a thin coat is better.

check.q: Where is it right to wax an edge?
choices: only where skating is allowed, like a skatepark ledge
check.why: Wax leaves marks and makes steps slippery, so wax only where skating is allowed.

lessons.title: Practice Without Rolling
lessons.mainIdea: Setting the board on the edge while standing still lets you feel the balance point before you add speed.
reading: Before rolling, learn what a grind feels like with the board still. Set your board on the curb so both trucks sit on the top corner and the wheels hang over the side you will ride from. Hold a friend's shoulder or a fence. Step your back foot over the back bolts, then your front foot over the front bolts. The bolts are the screw heads that hold the trucks to the deck.

Now feel where your weight must go. Lean too far toward the ground side and the board tips off. Lean toward the top of the curb and the wheels drop onto it. Somewhere in the middle, with your knees bent and your shoulders level, the board balances on the edge. That middle spot is the feeling you are hunting for when you are moving.

Next, try a rolling drill that is not a grind at all. Ride slowly next to the curb, almost parallel, and ollie up onto the flat top of the curb. Roll along the top and off the end. This teaches you to judge the distance and the timing. When that feels easy ten times in a row, start aiming a little lower, so your trucks meet the edge itself.

words.d: the screw heads on top of the deck that hold the trucks on; skaters place their feet over them
the spot where your weight sits so the board stays on the edge without tipping either way
a small practice move repeated to build one part of a skill

look.title: Standing on the Edge

Your back foot is over the back bolts and your front foot is over the front bolts. A friend's shoulder steadies you. You shift your hips an inch toward the ground side and feel the board start to tip. You shift back and it settles.

check.q: In the standing drill, where do both trucks rest?
choices: on the top corner of the curb
on top of the grip tape
check.why: The drill sets both trucks on the edge so you can feel the grind's balance.

check.q: Where should your front foot go in the standing drill?
choices: on the very tip of the tail
check.why: The reading places the front foot over the front bolts and the back foot over the back bolts.

check.q: Which rolling drill comes before aiming at the edge itself?
choices: jump down a set of stairs
ride the curb at top speed

check.why: Ollying onto the curb top teaches distance and timing before you aim at the edge.

lessons.title: The 50-50
lessons.mainIdea: In a 50-50, both trucks grind the edge at once with your weight centered between them.
reading: The *50-50* is the first grind most skaters learn. Both trucks grind the edge at the same time, so the weight is shared fifty-fifty. It came from pool skating in the late 1970s, when skaters ground the coping, the rounded edge at the top of a pool wall. On flat ground it is done on curbs, ledges and flat bars.

Here are the steps. First, roll toward the curb at a slow, steady speed, nearly parallel to it, with your feet in ollie position: back foot on the tail, front foot just behind the front bolts. Next, when your front wheels are close to the edge, ollie up and a little toward it. Then guide the board so both trucks land on the corner at once. Bend your knees as they land and keep your weight centered between the trucks.

Ride the edge with your shoulders lined up with the curb. At the end, let the board roll off the end and land with bent knees, rolling away. A common problem is landing with only the back truck on, which tips the nose down onto the top. The fix is to ollie a little higher and level the board in the air. Another is landing too far onto the top. Then come in closer to the edge before you pop.

words.d: a grind with both trucks on the edge at the same time, weight shared evenly
the rounded metal or concrete edge at the top of a ramp or pool wall
back foot on the tail and front foot just behind the front bolts, ready to pop

look.title: A 50-50, Step by Step
look.text: Step 1: Roll slowly beside the curb, almost parallel. Step 2: Feet in ollie position, knees bent. Step 3: Pop the tail with the back foot and slide the front foot up. Step 4: Level the board in the air and steer it toward the edge. Step 5: Both trucks land on the corner. Step 6: Knees stay bent, eyes on the far end. Step 7: Roll off the end and ride away.

check.q: What touches the edge in a 50-50?
check.why: In a 50-50 both trucks grind at once, sharing the weight evenly.

check.q: Where did skaters first grind coping in the late 1970s?
choices: on the rounded edges of pools
check.why: The 50-50 grew from pool skating, grinding the coping at the top of the wall.

check.q: Only your back truck keeps landing on the edge. What is the fix from the reading?
choices: ollie a little higher and level the board in the air
push much faster at the curb
look down at your front foot
check.why: Leveling the board in the air lets both trucks land at once.

lessons.title: The 5-0
lessons.mainIdea: A 5-0 grinds on the back truck only, balanced like a manual with the nose up.
reading: In a *5-0* (say five-oh), only the back truck grinds. The nose stays up in the air and the front truck hangs above the edge. If you have practiced a *manual*, balancing on the back wheels while rolling on flat ground, you already know the feeling. A 5-0 is a manual done on an edge instead of on the ground.

The steps begin like a 50-50. Roll toward the curb nearly parallel at a slow, steady speed. Ollie up toward the edge, but keep a little more weight on the back foot as you land, so the back truck meets the corner first and the nose stays up. Your back foot sits over the back bolts, not on the very end of the tail. Your front foot stays light over the front bolts, steering the nose level.

The hard part is the balance. If you lean too far back, the tail drags on the curb and the board stops. If you lean too far forward, the front truck drops and the trick turns into a 50-50. Aim to keep the nose a few inches up and steady. At the end, press the front foot down a little as the board rolls off, so both trucks come down together on the ground.

words.d: a grind on the back truck only, with the nose held up in the air
balancing on the back wheels while rolling, with the nose up off the ground
when the tail scrapes the surface because too much weight is on the back foot

look.title: Manual, Then 5-0
look.text: Picture two skaters. One rolls across flat ground with the nose a few inches up, balanced over the back wheels. The other rolls along a curb with the nose a few inches up, balanced over the back truck as it scrapes the edge. Their bodies look almost the same: knees bent, arms out, eyes ahead.
look.prompt: How long can you hold a manual on flat ground? Why might a longer manual help your 5-0?

check.q: Which part grinds in a 5-0?
check.why: A 5-0 is a grind on the back truck with the nose up.

check.q: In a 5-0, the tail drags and the board stops. What happened?
choices: the skater leaned too far back
the skater leaned too far forward
the front truck was too loose
check.why: Too much weight on the back foot drops the tail onto the edge, which stops the board.

check.q: Which flat-ground trick feels most like a 5-0?
check.why: A manual balances on the back wheels with the nose up, the same balance as a 5-0.

lessons.title: Angle and Speed
lessons.mainIdea: Come in at a shallow angle and a steady, comfortable speed so the trucks lock on and carry to the end.
reading: The *approach* is the path you ride toward the obstacle. For a 50-50 or 5-0, come in at a shallow angle, nearly parallel to the edge, but slightly toward it. A good picture is a door opened only a little. If you ride straight at the curb, the board will hit the edge and stop, or fly over the top. If you ride exactly parallel and far away, you cannot reach the edge when you pop.

Speed matters as much as angle. A friction force slows the board the whole time it grinds, so a board that arrives slowly stops partway. A board that arrives too fast is hard to steer onto the edge and hard to control at the end. Start at an easy rolling speed, a little faster than a brisk walk, and add a little speed on each try once you can land on the edge.

You can also choose a side. In a *frontside* grind your chest and toes face the edge as you approach. In a *backside* grind your back and heels face it. Both are normal, and each skater may feel more comfortable on one side first. Pick one side, practice it until it feels steady, then learn the other.

words.d: the path and speed a skater uses riding toward an obstacle
how fast the board is moving, measured in meters per second
a grind done with your chest and toes facing the edge as you approach
a grind done with your back and heels facing the edge as you approach

check.q: What happens if you ride straight at the curb instead of at a shallow angle?

check.q: Why does a board that arrives too slowly stop partway?
choices: friction slows it the whole time it grinds
check.why: Friction acts during the whole grind, so a slow board runs out of speed early.

check.q: In a frontside grind, what faces the edge as you approach?

lessons.title: The Boardslide
lessons.mainIdea: In a boardslide the board turns across the rail and the middle of the deck slides along it, between the trucks.
reading: In a *boardslide*, the board sits across the rail, crosswise, with the rail between the two trucks. The middle of the deck's underside slides along the metal. A low flat bar is the classic place to learn it, because the bar is narrow and slick. The board points across the bar while you slide along it.

Here are the steps. First, roll toward the flat bar nearly straight on, but just to one side of its end. Next, ollie and turn your shoulders and the board a quarter turn, so the board crosses over the bar. Then land with the bar under the middle of the deck, between your feet. Keep your knees bent and your weight right over the bar, with your head above it.

To come off, turn your shoulders back a quarter turn at the end of the bar, so the board points forward again, and roll away. A common problem is leaning away from the direction you are sliding. Your feet then shoot forward and you sit down. The fix is to keep your weight over the bar and your eyes on its end. Another is landing with a truck on the bar, which hangs up the board; ollie a little higher to clear it.

words.d: a slide with the board crosswise on a rail so the middle of the deck slides between the trucks
a straight metal rail set level and low on short legs, used for learning grinds and slides
when a truck or wheel catches on an obstacle and stops the board suddenly

look.title: From Above
look.text: Picture looking down from above a low flat bar. The skater rolls toward its end, pops and turns. Now the board forms a plus sign with the bar: board across, bar along. The bar sits under the middle of the deck, between the front and back trucks. The skater slides along the bar, then turns the board back in line and rolls away.
look.prompt: Draw the plus sign the board and bar make. Where are the two trucks in your drawing?

check.q: Which part of the board touches the rail in a boardslide?
choices: the middle of the deck, between the trucks
check.why: A boardslide has the rail under the middle of the deck.

check.q: How is the board turned compared to the rail in a boardslide?
check.why: The board turns a quarter turn so it crosses the rail.

check.q: What usually happens if you lean away from the slide's direction?
choices: your feet shoot forward and you sit down
check.why: Leaning away lets the board run out from under your feet.

lessons.title: The Noseslide
lessons.mainIdea: In a noseslide, the board turns a quarter turn and only the nose slides on the ledge.
reading: The *nose* is the front end of the deck, past the front truck. In a *noseslide*, you ollie up, turn the board a quarter turn, and set only the underside of the nose on the ledge. The rest of the board hangs off the ground side, and the back wheels stay in the air. A waxed ledge works better than a round rail for learning it, because the nose sits flat on top.

Here are the steps. First, roll toward the ledge nearly parallel at an easy speed. Next, pop an ollie and turn your shoulders and the board a quarter turn toward the ledge. Then press your front foot onto the nose so the nose lands on the top edge. Most of your weight should sit over the front foot. Keep your back foot light on the tail and your knees bent.

To come off, push lightly with the front foot and turn your shoulders back a quarter turn, so the board lines up with your path and rolls away. A common problem is not getting enough weight on the nose. The board then slips off right away. The fix is to lean forward over the front foot and look toward the end of the ledge. Another is turning too far, past a quarter turn, so you come off pointing the wrong way.

words.d: the front end of the deck, past the front truck
a slide with the board turned a quarter turn so only the nose rests on the ledge
a turn of about 90 degrees, so the board points across your path

look.title: Weight on the Front
look.text: Picture a skater in a noseslide on a low waxed ledge. The board points away from the ledge, crosswise to the path. Only the nose rests on the top edge. The front knee is bent deep and the front shoulder leans out over the nose. The back foot rests lightly on the tail, which floats in the air over the ground.
look.prompt: Stand on a board on carpet and shift most of your weight to your front foot. How does it change your balance?

check.q: Which part of the board rests on the ledge in a noseslide?
check.why: A noseslide sets only the underside of the nose on the ledge.

check.q: Where should most of your weight be during a noseslide?
check.why: The nose carries the slide, so most weight goes over the front foot.

check.q: In a noseslide, the board slips off right away. What is the likely cause?
choices: not enough weight on the nose
too much wax on the wheels
a helmet that is too loose
check.why: Without enough weight on the nose, it will not stay on the ledge.

lessons.title: The Tailslide
lessons.mainIdea: A tailslide sets the tail on the ledge with the board turned a quarter turn and the weight over the back foot.
reading: The *tail* is the back end of the deck, past the back truck, the part you pop for an ollie. A *tailslide* is the back-end partner of the noseslide. You ollie, turn the board a quarter turn, and set the underside of the tail on the top edge of the ledge. The front of the board points out over the ground and the front wheels hang in the air.

Here are the steps. First, ride toward the ledge nearly parallel at an easy, steady speed. Next, ollie a little higher than usual, because the tail must reach the top of the ledge. Then turn your shoulders and the board a quarter turn and press the tail down onto the edge with your back foot. Keep most of your weight over the back foot, with your front foot steadying the board over the front bolts.

To come off, turn your shoulders back a quarter turn and let the board drop to the ground pointing forward, with knees bent. A common problem is the tail landing below the top of the ledge, against its side. The board then stops hard. The fix is to pop higher and keep the front knee bent so the board levels out. Many skaters find the tailslide harder than the noseslide, because the slide happens behind them, where they cannot see it as easily.

words.d: the back end of the deck, past the back truck, which you pop for an ollie
a slide with the board turned a quarter turn so only the tail rests on the ledge
the quick snap of the tail against the ground that lifts the board into an ollie

look.title: Nose or Tail?
look.text: Picture two skaters side by side on the same ledge. Both boards are turned a quarter turn. The first skater leans forward and the nose rests on the edge; the tail floats over the ground. The second leans back and the tail rests on the edge; the nose floats over the ground. Same ledge, opposite ends, opposite weight.
look.prompt: Name each trick. Which foot carries most of the weight in each one?

check.q: Which part rests on the ledge in a tailslide?
check.why: A tailslide sets the underside of the tail on the ledge.

check.q: Which foot carries most of the weight in a tailslide?
check.why: The tail is under the back foot, so most weight goes there.

check.q: Why does a tailslide often need a slightly higher ollie?
choices: the nose must touch the ground
the tail must reach the top of the ledge
check.why: If the pop is low, the tail hits the side of the ledge instead of the top.

lessons.title: Look Where You Want to Go
lessons.mainIdea: Keeping your eyes on the end of the ledge keeps your shoulders, hips and weight lined up for the whole grind.
reading: Your body tends to follow your eyes. If you stare down at your front foot during a grind, your head drops and your shoulders tip forward. That moves your weight off the balance point, and the board slides off early. Coaches tell skaters to look at the end of the ledge or rail instead, the spot where they plan to roll off.

Looking ahead also lines up your *shoulders*. For a 50-50 or 5-0, your shoulders should point along the ledge, the same direction as your path. For a boardslide, noseslide or tailslide, your shoulders turn with the board for the slide, then turn back for the exit. Your head and eyes lead the turn, and your shoulders and hips follow.

The *exit* is how you leave the obstacle. On a low curb, the simplest exit is rolling off the end and landing with bent knees, both feet over the bolts. Plan your exit before you start the trick, and look at that spot from the very beginning. A skater who knows where the trick ends rides it with more confidence than one who is only thinking about getting on.

words.d: the upper body's line, which skaters point along the path to keep the board on course
the way a skater leaves an obstacle at the end of a grind or slide
keeping your weight over the part of the board that is holding you up

look.title: Two Sets of Eyes
look.text: Picture two skaters in a 50-50 on the same curb. The first stares at her front foot. Her chin drops, her shoulders round forward, and her board slides off the ground side after half a meter. The second looks at the end of the curb. Her chin is up, her shoulders point along the curb, and she rides to the end and rolls away.
look.prompt: On your next roll on flat ground, pick a spot ahead and keep your eyes on it. Does your board go where you look?

check.q: Where should your eyes be during a grind?
choices: on the end of the ledge
check.why: Looking at the end keeps the head up and the weight on the balance point.

check.q: In a 50-50, which way should your shoulders point?
choices: along the ledge, the way you are going
check.why: For truck grinds, the shoulders line up with the ledge and your path.

check.q: When should you plan your exit?
check.why: Planning the exit first lets you look at it and ride the trick with confidence.

lessons.title: Bailing Safely
lessons.mainIdea: A good bail means stepping off and running it out when you can, and falling low and rolling when you cannot.
reading: To *bail* is to leave the board on purpose when a trick goes wrong. Every skater bails many times while learning a grind. The safest bail is a step-off: as soon as the board stops or tips, step both feet onto the ground on the side away from the obstacle and jog a few steps. The board may roll away, so check that no one is in its path.

Sometimes there is no time to step off. Then fall small. Bend your knees and get low, so you drop a short distance. Tuck your chin. Let your body roll onto the meaty side of your shoulder, your hip or your back instead of stopping all at once. Slide on your knee pads if you fall forward. Do not throw out locked, straight arms to catch yourself. Wrist injuries are among the most common skateboarding injuries, and wrist guards help prevent them.

Fear is a normal signal, not a weakness. If a trick scares you, make it smaller. Go back to the standing drill, lower the speed, or practice ollying onto the curb top again. A short practice session with many small, controlled tries builds a grind faster than a few big, scary ones. Stop when you are tired, because tired legs land badly.

words.d: to leave the board on purpose when a trick is going wrong
a bail where you put both feet on the ground and jog away from the board
to crouch low, tuck and roll so a fall is short and spread out

lock your arms straight and catch yourself
stay on and lean back hard
jump as high as you can
check.why: A step-off puts you on your feet with no fall at all.

check.q: Why should you not catch a fall with locked, straight arms?
choices: wrist injuries are among the most common, and locked arms take the whole hit
it makes the board roll faster
check.why: Locked arms put all the force into the wrists, a very common injury.

lessons.title: A Step-by-Step Practice Plan
lessons.mainIdea: Grinds and slides come in a sensible order, each one building on the skills of the one before.
reading: Grinds and slides build on each other, so the order you learn them matters. A common path starts with a steady rolling ollie, then ollying onto the curb top, then the 50-50. The 50-50 teaches you to land on an edge with your weight centered. Next comes the 5-0, which adds the manual's balance on the back truck.

Slides usually come after you are comfortable on your trucks. A boardslide on a low flat bar teaches the quarter turn on and off. The noseslide and tailslide add turning plus putting most of your weight over one end. Each new trick reuses a skill you already have: the ollie, the quarter turn, a manual's balance, or looking at the end of the obstacle.

Keep each practice short and focused. Choose one trick and one side, frontside or backside, for a session. Warm up with ollies on flat ground. Count your clean tries instead of your falls. When one trick works on a low curb most of the time, it is ready for a slightly longer or slightly higher ledge at the skatepark, one small change at a time.

words.d: learning skills in an order where each step builds on the one before
easy skating at the start of a session that gets your body ready
an attempt where you land the trick and ride away in control

Step 5: 5-0 on a low curb. Step 6: Boardslide on a low flat bar. Step 7: Noseslide on a waxed ledge. Step 8: Tailslide on a waxed ledge.

check.q: What skill does the 5-0 add on top of the 50-50?
choices: a manual's balance on the back truck
check.why: The 5-0 balances on the back truck, like a manual.

check.q: What does the reading suggest you count during a session?
check.why: Counting clean tries keeps the focus on progress.

review.q: What is the difference between a grind and a slide?
choices: a grind rides on the deck; a slide rides on the trucks
a grind uses wheels; a slide uses grip tape
a grind rides on the trucks; a slide rides on the deck
review.why: Grinds scrape the metal trucks; slides rub the wooden deck.

review.q: Which trick uses the back truck only, with the nose up?
review.why: The 5-0 grinds on the back truck with the nose held up.

review.q: Why does a skater rub a thin coat of wax on a curb?
review.why: Wax makes the edge slicker, so the board keeps going.

review.q: In a boardslide, where is the rail?
choices: under the middle of the deck, between the trucks
between the wheels on one truck
review.why: The board crosses the rail so the middle of the deck slides on it.

review.q: What is the best approach for a first 50-50?
choices: straight at the curb at top speed
a shallow angle at an easy, steady speed
review.why: A shallow angle lets you reach the edge, and an easy speed keeps control.

review.q: Which foot carries most of the weight in a noseslide?
review.why: The nose is under the front foot, so the weight goes there.

review.q: Where should your eyes be as you grind?
choices: on the end of the ledge
review.why: Looking at the end keeps your weight and shoulders lined up.

review.q: What should you do with your arms in a fall?
choices: lock them straight to stop the fall
keep them bent and roll instead of catching yourself with locked arms
review.why: Rolling spreads the fall; locked arms send the force into the wrists.
